title: Why do XRPL payments need destination tags?
abstract: Primary-source guide to why do xrpl payments need destination tags?. Includes integration considerations and evidence boundaries.
body:
A destination tag tells a recipient's off-ledger system which beneficiary or purpose to credit when several customers share an XRPL account. It is a 32-bit unsigned integer, not a separate wallet or authorization credential. Source tags identify the originator or return-routing context. The ledger carries these values, while the receiving business interprets them. [1]

Hosted accounts can use tags to avoid funding a distinct ledger account for each customer. An X-address encodes a classic address and tag together. A recipient can require destination tags, but that does not prove that any supplied tag belongs to the intended customer. Application-side mapping remains necessary; a syntactically valid payment can still be operationally misrouted. [1]

I recommend treating address and tag as one verified payment destination in an agent's quote and signing policy. Preserve the tag through serialization, display and recovery. Do not let model-generated prose supply a substitute value. For a returned payment, the documentation recommends using the incoming source tag as the outgoing destination tag. Reconcile that routing with the original transaction instead of guessing from the sender's display name. [1]

Exercise missing, unknown and correctly mapped tags in integration tests. Distinguish a ledger rejection from a payment accepted by the ledger but not credited to a hosted customer. Avoid publishing a customer directory in tag metadata: the documentation notes that predictable assignment can reveal relationships. These recommendations follow the tag model and should be checked against the receiving service's actual deposit instructions before deployment. [1]
